newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope, refreshed by mountains, returns to the road.
newsitem.headline: Pope, refreshed by mountains, returns to the road.

text.p: Pope John Paul, refreshed after a private rest day in his beloved Tatra mountains, returns to public view on Friday during his gruelling tour of his home country of Poland.
"He feels well, he rests and it seems that this land does him good," Bishop Tadeusz Pieronek, secretary-general of the Polish bishops conference, told a news conference on Thursday night.

The 77-year-old Pontiff was due to preside at an open-air beatification mass on Friday morning in the mountain town of Zakopane at which two Polish nuns who lived in the 19th and 20th centuries will be put on the road to sainthood.
The ceremony was expected to draw many thousands of people to see the Pope in the idyllic area where he used to relax and meditate as a young man and later as a bishop and cardinal.

The Pope had no public engagements on Thursday, the sixth day of his visit. Instead he was flown by helicopter for more than two hours over favourite mountain walks and a river where he used to canoe.
The helicopter put down briefly near a small church in the mountains so that he could bless a group of waiting people.
"The Pope was happy to revisit a series of places that are dear to him," Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said. "It's very clear that he is very happy to be home."
He made a second outing, this time by car, in the afternoon from the church-owned retreat in Zakopane where Polish and Vatican security officials jealously guarded his privacy.

The Tatra region of sweeping vistas is precious to the sometimes frail Pope, who appears reinvigorated by the scent and feel of his homeland and the rapturous welcome of more than a million Poles since his arrival on Saturday.
During the visit, one of his longest to a single country, he has prodded Poles to excercise their new economic and political freedoms properly.
Realising that people are themselves questioning their country's direction, he has pulled no punches on some of the most burning issues dividing them, chiefly abortion.
He railed against the practice in the central city of Kalisz on Wednesday, saying economically and culturally successful societies were still barbarian if they allowed it.

Whether abortion should remain liberalised or be restricted again has become a key issue in the campaign for September's elections, in which a powerful alliance centred around the pro-Catholic Solidarity union is challenging the ruling ex-communists.
But Bishop Pieronek said the Pope was not speaking politically but was delivering "a message of morality targetted at the human conscience" when he talked about abortion.
"The matter of abortion is a question of morality, ethics and human rights, not politics," Pieronek said.
Vatican officials say that each time the Pope visits Poland he does so with the realisation that it might be his last trip to his homeland.

But Pieronek said the Polish bishops had plans to invite him back next year. He said there were a number of dioceses that could not be be fitted into this visit, including Gdansk, the port where the Solidarity union was born in 1980.
